headline: Iran Hormuz draft ban on US and Israel pushes oil higher
tldr: Iran published a draft plan restricting Strait of Hormuz transit, banning the US and Israel and blocking others pending compensation.
S&P 500 closed Friday at 7,757 and VIX at 14.90, suggesting markets are not yet pricing in the Hormuz risk.
UK home insurance market forecast to return a 103% NCR in 2026, with average premiums expected to fall to around £320.
Head of Data salaries frequently exceed £90,000, with AI and data leadership roles seeing salary growth of up to 6%.
BP has put its UK North Sea business up for sale, signalling further retreat of major oil firms from domestic extraction.

sections.title: Markets
sections.body:
**Markets — Sunday 9 August 2026**

Today's session is the first full trading day since Friday's close. The pre-fetched data shows modest but broadly positive early moves — this is what's actually new since yesterday's briefing.

The dominant new wrinkle is **oil creeping back up**. 
Oil rose on Friday after Iran published a restrictive draft plan for the Strait of Hormuz
, and 
under that apparent draft, the US and Israel would be banned from transit, with other nations blocked until compensation is paid.
 That walked back some of the optimism from earlier in the week and is the clearest risk to the bullish rate narrative — higher oil feeds into core PCE, which feeds into Fed expectations.


US markets closed Friday with the S&P 500 at 7,757.64 (+0.62%), Nasdaq at 26,690.62 (+1.30%), and the VIX at 14.90
 — a low-fear reading that suggests the Iran draft hasn't rattled confidence much yet. 
The FTSE 100 finished Friday at 10,921.68, another step into record territory
, though today's pre-fetched data has it at 10,901 — a small consolidation, likely reflecting the oil tick-up weighing on energy heavyweights.

In Asia, the Nikkei closed Friday at 65,607 (-0.12%). 
Broader sentiment was weighed by the oil rebound following renewed Hormuz tensions.
 Today's IJPN +0.78% suggests a partial bounce.

In the portfolio, ASML +2.15% is the standout — semiconductor equipment benefiting from the tech-friendly rate backdrop. AMD -1.21% continues its post-earnings drift. BAE +0.91% and QinetiQ +1.19% remain firm on defence spending expectations.

**Watch:** the Hormuz draft plan is the key live variable — any hardening or softening of Iran's position will move oil directly, repricing inflation expectations and by extension the whole equity rally.

sections.body:
**GW1 — Deadline: Friday 21 Aug, 17:30 BST**

**Prices**

Prices remain locked until after Friday's deadline. No market movement to act on — squad construction is the only lever.

**Injuries & doubts**

The pre-fetched data flags several players to resolve before Friday:

- **Šeško, Tielemans & Martínez (Man Utd)** — all 75% chance of playing. 
None should be treated as a guaranteed GW1 starter.
 Plan around their absence, treat starts as a bonus.
- **Kroupi Jr (Bournemouth)** — foot injury, unknown return. Confirmed avoid.
- **Garner (Everton)** — expected back 22 Aug, i.e. after the deadline. Avoid.
- **Wissa (Brentford, £7.5m)** — 
will play no part in Brentford's opener; manager Keith Andrews confirmed he will not take part against Nottingham Forest.

- **Morgan Rogers (Aston Villa, £7.0m)** — 
ankle injury from the Roma friendly on 6 August, though he has returned to training and will be monitored ahead of Saturday's opener against Newcastle.

- **Kelleher (Brentford, £4.5m)** — 
doubt for GW1 after a knock forced him out of the Borussia Mönchengladbach friendly on 8 August.


**Differentials**

- 
Kai Havertz is the standout differential pick, sitting at just 6.9% ownership with the best differential score of the entire pool.

- 
Havertz and Mateta project as season-long differentials rather than one-week punts, with strong xGI/90 and workable fixtures.

- 
Gabriel is a genuine differential captain option for the brave, given his set-piece threat and clean-sheet upside.

- Sunderland assets (
who begin against Ipswich before hosting Fulham
) are circulating as short-horizon differentials, though 
the difficulty ramps up from GW3, with Arsenal and Man City arriving within the opening six gameweeks.

sections.title: Data & BI
sections.body:
The search results don't surface genuinely new BigQuery or dbt stories from this week that weren't already covered yesterday. The freshest Power BI item is the semantic model settings pane going live in August. I'll focus on what's actually new since yesterday's section and avoid repeating anything already covered.

**Data & BI** · 9 August 2026

The big July Power BI story, PBIR/Desktop Bridge/dbt trust figures, and Snowflake Semantic View Autopilot were all in yesterday's briefing. One item is genuinely new this morning.

**Power BI — semantic model settings pane now live**


From August, opening settings for a semantic model in the Power BI Service takes you to a new inline pane rather than the full settings page — it opens beside your content, so you can update refresh schedules, credentials, and other options without leaving your workspace.
 
Everything configurable on the legacy page remains available; you can switch back to the legacy page from within the pane if needed.


Small UX change, but worth flagging for anyone who has documented admin or on-call runbooks that reference the old settings page path — screenshotted steps will now be wrong.

**dbt — the analytics engineer role is being explicitly redefined**


dbt Labs' own framing is blunt: an analytics engineer who spends 2026 competing with AI on code production will find the role shrinking; one who focuses on business judgment, context design, and governance ownership will find it expanding.
 
The argument is that AI agents need context to reason reliably, and in a well-structured dbt project that comes from MetricFlow metric definitions, column-level lineage, model documentation, and schema contracts.
 Worth using as a framing device when making the case for semantic layer investment internally.

sections.title: Career & Data Leadership
sections.body:
**Hiring & market conditions**


Data roles are holding up against the broader softness — new postings are up 7.7% year-on-year
, and 
the talent market faces a distinct scarcity of digital expertise, pushing salaries sharply higher for leadership roles in AI, cloud, and data specifically.
 
Some organisations have slowed hiring or merged data teams with software or analytics functions
 — worth watching if you're assessing a role's structural stability before accepting.

**Salary — Head of Data level**


Head of Data roles frequently exceed £90,000, particularly where responsibility includes governance, reporting strategy, and enterprise data architecture oversight.
 
Salaries across data are rising 2–4% on average, with stronger growth of up to 6% across AI, data, and cybersecurity.
 That upper band is now the one to benchmark against in any negotiation, not the midpoint.

**Leadership lens — visibility over capability**

The sharpest practical point doing the rounds: 
the defining risk for data leaders in 2026 is that technical credibility alone is no longer sufficient — the executives driving real impact are those who lead the business *through* data, not just lead the data function.
 
2026 is a turning point: justifying initiatives on technological innovation alone is no longer enough — leaders must demonstrate measurable business value and scale AI from pilots to enterprise-wide implementation.


- 
Senior data leaders now need strong business acumen, AI governance expertise, change management capabilities, and the ability to build partnerships across organisational silos.

- 
BARC's practitioner survey put data quality management and data security at the top of the priority rankings for 2026
 — both are governance plays, reinforcing the interview signal flagged yesterday.
- 
The talent challenge in 2026 is not just about hiring specialists — it is about enabling the broader organisation to work effectively with data and AI.
 How you frame that team-enablement story matters as much as your technical pedigree.

sections.title: UK Insurance
sections.body:
**UK Insurance**

Two stories have moved since yesterday — home market profitability and a new retail distribution play — plus a relevant Flood Re development.

**Home market: back in the red, premiums beginning to turn**


EY forecasts the UK home insurance market will return to loss-making territory in 2026, with an NCR of 103% — £1.03 paid out in claims and expenses for every £1 of premium.
 
Average written premiums are expected to fall 3% by year-end, bringing a typical policy to around £320 versus £330 in 2025.
 However, there are early signs of a floor: 
home premiums rose 1% in June — the first notable monthly increase after a long run of falling prices — following declines of 0.4% in April and 1.2% in May, per Defaqto's market pricing data.


**Distribution: IKEA enters home insurance via Urban Jungle**


IKEA has entered the UK home insurance market through a partnership with insurtech Urban Jungle — the retailer's first collaboration with an insurance provider.
 
Policies are designed around flexibility and online management, with customers able to purchase digitally in minutes on monthly rolling terms.
 The pattern mirrors the John Lewis move: a high-footfall retail brand using an insurtech platform to enter personal lines without building underwriting capability. Worth watching which capacity provider sits behind Urban Jungle on this.

**Flood Re: levy and loss limit raised**


From 1 July 2026, Flood Re increased its annual levy on home insurers to £160m (from £135m) and raised its statutory loss limit from £100m to £250m.
 Higher levy = direct cost line for any home insurer writing flood-exposed business.

sections.title: Milton Keynes
sections.body:
**Events — diary these**

- **📅 12–16 Oct** — 
MK Tech Week returns 12–16 October, building on last year's 23,000 attendees across 30+ events.
 
The theme this year is "Sovereign Technology" — UK control over critical tech, data and digital infrastructure.


- **📅 15 Oct** — 
Flagship one-day conference and expo at Unity Place: keynotes, panels and networking for business leaders, policymakers, researchers and investors.
 
Partners confirmed include The Open University, MK:U, MK College Group, HMGCC, BSI, Serve Robotics and Bletchley Park.
 Full programme still to be announced — watch [miltonkeynestechweek.com](https://miltonkeynestechweek.com/).

**Local news**

- **Roads.** 
MK City Council is investing over £6 million in this year's road resurfacing programme, with eleven roads being fully resurfaced this month
 — delivery on the pothole/roads commitment from the Council Plan, so worth noting if your commute takes you across any of the affected routes.

- **Skills investment.** 
MK College is set to receive £410,000 from the City Council to deliver specialist adult training in health and social care, construction, logistics and the creative industries.


- **Employment.** 
Payrolled employment in MK fell 0.2% in the year to June 2026 — around 308 fewer workers — though the monthly figure was broadly flat.
 A modest dip, but one to track given the broader data jobs market.

sections.title: News
sections.body:
I was unable to retrieve sufficiently fresh and verified headlines from today, 9 August 2026, to write a properly sourced News section. The search results I was able to gather are mostly a few days old (largely 3–6 August) and don't reflect what has actually broken this morning. Publishing a briefing built on stale or unverifiable claims — particularly one presented as today's news — risks being misleading.

What I can responsibly draw from the results to give you useful context:

---

**UK Politics & Economy**

- 
The Burnham government has declined to rule out higher bank taxes ahead of a forthcoming Budget, fuelling speculation in what Bloomberg describes as "silly season" bank-tax talk.


- 
Markets have been watching the new Burnham administration closely for signals on fiscal direction; sentiment stabilised somewhat after the Chancellor confirmed the first Budget will be on 28 October, giving investors a clearer timetable.


- 
Britain's new defence spending ambitions are running into fiscal constraints
, with the government yet to set out how higher commitments will be funded.

- 
BP has put its UK North Sea business up for sale
 — a significant signal of the ongoing retreat of major oil companies from domestic extraction.

- 
UK unemployment held at 4.9% in the three months to May, unchanged from the prior quarter but 0.2 percentage points higher than a year ago.
 
Job vacancies for April–June fell to 712,000 — roughly half the 2022 peak — with the ONS attributing the decline to employer reluctance to hire.


**World**

- 
Israel's far-right government, facing a possible loss of power in an October election, has accelerated West Bank settlement activity, legalising past settlements and approving new ones in areas meant to be under Palestinian civil control.


- 
An explosive device attached to a drone was found near a runway at Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany, discovered by an airport employee and examined by police.


- 
In Pakistan, candidates backed by Nawaz Sharif's PML-N party won 24 of the 34 seats decided in the first two phases of regional voting, according to the election commission.


---

**⚠️ Caveat:** Most of these items are from 4–7 August. I was unable to retrieve verified breaking news from this morning (9 August). I'd recommend cross-checking BBC News or Reuters directly before your first meeting for anything time-sensitive.
